Brand & Design Guideline

Visual quick reference for partners, vendors & contractors

Rhapsody · October 2026 · For approved external use

How to use this guide

This is Rhapsody's visual system: logo, color, type, graphic devices (the dots and light glows), photography, buttons, and the common layout patterns — with the rules and correct examples for each. Work from these pages when producing anything that carries the Rhapsody brand.

Every example here is live HTML rendered from the real design tokens, so colors, type, and spacing are exact. Use the Contents below to jump to a section.

Master art is included with this package. The approved logos, monograms, big-dot and scattered-dot device files are provided as separate SVG/PNG files in the accompanying rhapsody-brand-assets folder — use those masters as-is (never rebuild or restyle them). Anything not in the asset folder is available on request from your Rhapsody contact.

Brand expression

Rhapsody should feel technologically advanced, intelligent, precise, established, and human. The visual system must communicate innovation without sacrificing the confidence and trust expected of healthcare infrastructure. AI should feel embedded in the system, not represented as novelty or decoration.

Precise, not playful

Favor ordered systems, confident typography, controlled color, and intentional spacing over whimsical or decorative treatments.

Advanced, not sci-fi

Signal modern technology through data, connection, orchestration, product UI, and abstract system imagery rather than futuristic clichés.

Human, not juvenile

Use credible real people and professional environments. Avoid cartoon-like characters, cute metaphors, or illustration styles that reduce enterprise credibility.

Confident, not loud

Let white space, hierarchy, and a restrained palette carry the brand. Do not add color or devices merely to fill open space.

Color

Rhapsody Blue is the primary color, used most prominently. Rhapsody Navy, light blue, and teal are secondary. Purple and orange are restricted tertiary accents, not general-purpose layout colors. A standard Rhapsody layout should usually contain no tertiary colors at all. Full-page backgrounds stay white, Rhapsody Blue, or Rhapsody Navy; light gray and gray-blue are for content modules, not full-page fills.

Text color

Body copy uses only white, Rhapsody Navy, or black. Work down the list in order.

  • Rhapsody Navy is the default text color. On light backgrounds, set body copy and headings in Rhapsody Navy (#0B2C47) rather than black. Navy is the on-brand dark and clears contrast on white easily.
  • Black is a fallback, not a default. Reach for black (#050F19) only when navy fails a contrast requirement, or in print that can’t reproduce navy (single-color or limited-ink jobs). Otherwise, navy.
  • Rhapsody Blue is the accent on light. Use it for emphasis, links, and one accent word in a headline, not for running body copy.
  • On dark backgrounds, text is white. For blue accents on navy, the two blues split by size—see “Rhapsody Blue on navy” below.
  • No tertiary color in type: teal, purple, and orange are never used for body copy, headings, eyebrows, or labels. Two exceptions: on navy, teal may set an eyebrow, label, small icon, or actionlink (6.7:1 on navy — see Teal in small applications below), and an H3 may take a secondary color where contrast allows (navy on light; light blue or teal on dark). On light grounds there is no teal type of any kind: automation actionlinks stay Rhapsody Blue, and the teal cue is carried by a nearby accent (module accent line, tick, seam). H1, H2, body copy, and captions stay within the copy colors above.
  • Dark gray for supporting text. Dark gray (#7E858C) is allowed for secondary/supporting copy on white—subheads, support lines, captions—where a softer, de-emphasized read is wanted. Body copy still stays navy or black.
  • Color spaces: digital uses HEX or RGB; print uses CMYK or Pantone. For print, Rhapsody Blue is CMYK 100 50 0 0 (set it explicitly, don’t auto-convert the hex).
Default palette hierarchy

Most layouts should use White/Navy + Rhapsody Blue, with one optional secondary accent (Light Blue or Teal) only when needed. No more than three brand colors per layout, and reaching the maximum is not a goal. Purple and Orange do not count as freely available third colors; they appear only where another rule explicitly authorizes them. The multicolor fluid dot pattern and data visualizations remain controlled exceptions.

No custom gradients

Brand color is applied flat. Don’t create or add gradients—no color-to-color blends, ramps, or fades in backgrounds, fills, type, or shapes. The one approved exception is the soft glow of the Aurora light device (see Light devices); reach for it anywhere a gradient might feel warranted, and nowhere else.

Color accessibility

Accessibility requirements depend on the type of content. Use the thresholds below and then apply the brand-usage rules; a color pairing that technically passes contrast is not automatically an approved Rhapsody treatment.

  • Normal text: minimum contrast ratio 4.5:1.
  • Large text: minimum 3:1 (approximately 24px regular, or 18.5px bold and above).
  • UI components and meaningful graphic elements: minimum 3:1 against adjacent colors.
  • Decorative graphics: contrast requirements do not apply only when the element conveys no information.

Rhapsody Blue on navy

On navy (#0B2C47), default to light blue (#B4D8FF) for text — it reads about 9.7:1 and stays legible at any size, including the two-tone headline highlight. Don’t set text in Rhapsody Blue on navy: at 3.75:1 it only clears large sizes, and next to other colors on the dark ground it reads weak. Keep Rhapsody Blue on navy for large graphics, bars, blocks, and big dots, not type. A designer may override for a specific case where blue text genuinely reads well.

When to use which on navy

  • Light blue on navy: all text — headlines, body copy, captions, labels, accent and secondary lines, the two-tone headline highlight, thin rules, small icons, and small dots. This is the default for anything that reads as type on navy.
  • Rhapsody Blue on navy: large graphics only — bars, blocks, big dots, and sizable brand shapes where the blue stays vibrant. Not for text.
  • Designer override: blue text on navy is allowed only where a designer judges it genuinely reads well in a specific layout; otherwise light blue.

Teal in small applications

Small teal elements on light grounds keep failing contrast checks, and the common “fix”—darkening the teal—creates an off-brand second teal. The rule that prevents it: when a teal application fails contrast, change the ground or the role, never the hex. Teal (#23C5BF) reads at 6.7:1 on navy (passes at any size) and 2.1:1 on white (fails at any size), so the ground decides the role.

The rules

  • One teal. #23C5BF is the only teal. Never darken, tint, or theme-convert it to pass a contrast check — a “fixed” teal is an off-brand color.
  • Teal type lives on navy. Eyebrows, labels, actionlinks, and small icons may be teal on navy (6.7:1). This is the only ground where teal carries type.
  • On light grounds, teal is an accent, not a message. Use the teal tick (a 16×3px bar before a navy label), the module accent line, the teal seam, a pathway top edge, or structured dots. The text beside it carries the meaning in navy; the accent carries the color. Links stay Rhapsody Blue.
  • Meaningful teal graphics on light (a chart series, a status mark) need direct navy labels so nothing rides on the teal alone; add a thin navy keyline if the shape must read crisply at small sizes. Purely decorative teal (seams, ticks, dots, device glows) is exempt from contrast thresholds.
Teal is immutable

If a teal application fails an accessibility check, the hue is never the thing that changes. Move the element to navy, or demote the teal to an accent beside navy text. One teal, everywhere, always #23C5BF.

Test pairings with the WebAIM Contrast Checker or the EightShapes Contrast Grid.

Corners & shape

Two different rounded shapes do two different jobs, keep them separate. The fully rounded pill is for CTAs only (see Buttons and CTAs). Rounded corners are welcome for framing content, modules, cards, charts, callouts, and image frames, across webpages, PowerPoint slides, and editorial layouts. The recommendation below is how we do that most on brand.

Recommended: square the top, round the bottom

For framing modules and components, square off the top two corners and round the bottom two. The sleekest, most on-brand frame: engineered at the top, settled at the base. Use it as the default frame for content blocks, and keep the treatment consistent across a page or deck.

Module frame

Squared top, rounded bottom (12px).

✓ Recommended

Default for content blocks.

Chart / uniform

All four corners rounded (12px).

✓ Also fine

Charts and dense grids where a uniform frame suits.

Over-rounded

Pill-like radius on a module.

✕ Off-brand

The full pill radius is for CTAs only.

  • Pill (border-radius: 999px) = CTAs only. Never frame a module, card, chart, or image with it.
  • Module frame: square the top two corners, round the bottom two to about 12px (border-radius: 0 0 12px 12px). All four corners rounded (~12px) or fully square is also fine, for example charts and dense grids.
  • One treatment per page or deck, don’t mix squared-top frames with fully rounded ones in the same view.

Pathways

Rhapsody color-codes distinct paths so a user always knows which one they are on. Give each path or journey its own color and carry it as a wayfinding cue across every surface, so the color itself signals the path. This is a foundation for theming any set of parallel journeys, not a one-off section accent.

The directive

Assign each path a color and hold it end to end, across a page, a deck, a nav branch, a whole journey. Carry it as the cue wherever a surface belongs to the path: the module accent line, the eyebrow, in-context links and buttons, diagrams, and section theming. Default to blue when a surface is neutral or spans paths.

How to assign path colors

  • One color per path, held across its journey. A path reads the same color everywhere it appears, page, deck, and nav branch, so the cue stays predictable.
  • Assign in a fixed order so coding stays consistent as paths are added: blue → teal → purple → orange → light blue → navy.
  • Default to blue for neutral surfaces, or ones that span more than one path.
1 · Blue
2 · Teal
3 · Purple
4 · Orange
5 · Light blue
6 · Navy

Assign in order and hold each path’s color across its whole journey.

Where the cue appears

  • Website and navigation. Path landing pages and their sections theme to the path color, so moving into a branch is visible at a glance.
  • Module accent line. Takes the path color (see Layout and spacing for the device spec).
  • Eyebrows and links. In-context kickers, text links, and the CTA arrow take the path color. Feature icons stay in the blue family (navy, Rhapsody blue, light blue), never the path color, so the cue is carried by the accent line, eyebrow, and links, not the icons. On white, a light path color like teal drops to the line only; keep teal copy off white (see Color, Text on teal).
  • Content and diagrams. Path-specific decks, one-pagers, and diagrams carry the color consistently end to end.

Example: Build and Automate

The clearest current application is the two Rhapsody pillars, the first two colors in the sequence. Build the infrastructure is Rhapsody Blue; Automate the work is Teal. It shows the system in practice: each pillar holds its color across its whole journey, on the website, in path-specific content, and in section theming.

Build the infrastructure

Build on proven interoperability.

Path color: Rhapsody Blue #1A81F4. The blue accent line, eyebrow, links, and icons signal a build surface.

Automate the work

Automate the work around the data.

Path color: Teal #23C5BF. Teal cues the automate surface through the line; the eyebrow and heading stay navy.

Do
  • Give each path one color and hold it across its full journey, page, deck, and nav branch.
  • Default to blue for neutral surfaces or ones that span paths.
  • Add colors in the fixed order only when a genuine new path exists.
  • In the pillar example, keep Build blue and Automate teal wherever the two appear together.
Don’t
  • Swap or mix path colors, or switch a path’s color mid-journey.
  • Set teal, or any light path color, as small copy on white; the cue is the line or fill.
  • Invent a new color for a path, or reorder the sequence.
  • Theme a neutral, cross-path surface to one path’s color.

Layout and spacing

Layouts should always breathe. A few simple rules keep graphics and documents clean and consistent.

Margins and padding

Margins are the empty safe zone at the outer edge of a composition or page. Padding is the breathing room around and between the objects inside it, graphics, charts, images, text boxes, and callouts. They are set separately, and the right amount differs by application.

Outer margin (the safe zone)

For a self-contained graphic, a hero, ad, or social post, keep a clear margin of about 6 to 7 percent of the shorter side, with no copy, photo, or logo inside it (roughly a 40px margin on a 600px-wide graphic, scaling proportionally). That figure is correct for single graphics; multi-page documents follow their application’s page-margin convention instead.

  • Web: use 6–7% for self-contained graphics. Responsive page containers use a consistent gutter of about 24–40px on desktop and 16–20px on mobile.
  • PowerPoint (16:9): keep all content inside a safe margin of about 0.4–0.5in from every slide edge (roughly 5–6% of the 7.5in height). Align titles and footers to that same margin.
  • Word and print documents: use standard page margins of about 1in (never below 0.75in). Document margins are intentionally wider than the 6–7% graphic rule; don’t shrink them to match it.

Object padding (space around and between objects)

Every object, a chart, image, table, text box, or callout, keeps clear space around it so nothing touches or crowds. Hold a consistent minimum:

  • Web: at least 16–24px between objects and between an object and nearby text; container/card inner padding at least 16–24px.
  • PowerPoint: at least 0.2–0.3in between objects and between an object and its title or caption.
  • Word: at least 0.1–0.15in of wrap spacing around figures and tables, with a blank line above and below.
  • Never let a graphic, dot pattern, or glow touch or run under text; keep that gap at least the outer margin.

Rule of thumb: the 6–7% figure is the outer safe margin for a single graphic. Padding between objects is a separate, smaller gutter that keeps a busy layout legible. When in doubt, add space.

Text alignment

Default copy to left alignment. A consistent left edge is easiest to scan, so body copy, captions, lists, and any multi-line label set flush left. Center alignment is the exception, reserved for a short header, eyebrow, or single-line callout where centering genuinely reads better, never for running copy or anything that wraps to more than a line or two.

Separator line (the seam)

The seam is a tool to break up color blocking: a thin rule that marks the boundary where two sections of different colors meet, such as a navy band above a white body on a hero or email header. That is its rule, it must separate two different-colored sections; never run a seam inside a single color field or on a standalone piece (an ad or social post) where there is no color change. Keep it thin and full-width.

The seam color is teal, Rhapsody blue, navy, or light blue — pick the one that stays distinct from both sections it divides. Teal is the common choice where a navy band meets a light body; on a white or light band, Rhapsody blue (preferred for digital) or navy reads cleanly; light blue works as a quiet seam on navy.

Teal seam on a navy band (default).

White band: Rhapsody Blue (or navy) seam.

Module accent line (H2 sections)

Section modules led by an H2 open with a short horizontal accent line set directly above the heading, or above the eyebrow where one is present. It signals the start of a new content module and gives each section a consistent, engineered entry point.

The platform

Build on proven
interoperability.
  • Dimensions: 44px wide × 3px tall, 2px corner radius. One per module, tied to the primary H2, never repeated on sub-cards or stretched full-width.
  • Spacing: sits above the eyebrow/H2 with about 20–22px below it before the heading.
  • Color follows the pathway (default to blue for neutral surfaces), applied to the line only. Hold one accent color across a whole activation. The full color logic lives in Pathways.

Typography

Poppins is the primary typeface; IBM Plex Mono (weights 400 and 500) is the support face, for eyebrows and technical annotations (see below).

  • Fallback — Arial wherever Poppins can’t load, notably email (most clients won’t render Poppins) and some documents and devices. Set the stack 'Poppins', Arial, sans-serif and design so the layout still holds in Arial. Never bake copy into an image just to force the font.
  • One weight for the hierarchy — H2–H4 and all body copy in Poppins Regular (400); the hero and H1 step up to Poppins Medium (500) for a little more presence.
  • Medium (500) also handles small emphasis (labels, buttons) and short standalone “moment” headlines (see Stronger headlines for moments).

Stronger headlines for moments

The exception to the single-weight scale is a short, standalone headline that marks a moment or a step in a journey rather than leading a block of narrative copy. With only a few words and no supporting paragraph to lend it weight, a Regular headline reads thin, so step it up to Poppins Medium (500). Reserve this for confirmation and milestone screens, a submitted form, a completed step, not for section or narrative headlines. Use one per screen, paired with a short Regular supporting line.

Do: Medium for a standalone moment
You’re in!

Thanks for completing the survey. Watch your inbox for what’s next.

Don’t: Regular headline reads weak
You’re in!

A few words in Regular float without a narrative around them.

Eyebrows (kicker labels)

The small label above a headline (the eyebrow or kicker) sets in IBM Plex Mono.

Interoperability platform

Headline follows in Poppins

On light: IBM Plex Mono 500.

Interoperability platform

Headline follows in Poppins

On dark: IBM Plex Mono 500.

  • All caps, always.
  • IBM Plex Mono Medium (500). Regular 400 is acceptable where 500 renders heavy at very small sizes.
  • Size roughly 12–13px, sitting above the headline with clear space between.
  • Add letter-spacing so the caps don’t look cramped (see Leading & tracking for the value).
  • Markup: usually a <p> or <span>, not a heading. Exception: on product or landing pages the eyebrow may be the <h1> (the product name) when that reads better for SEO than a longer, stylized hero headline.
  • Avoid: Poppins for eyebrows, bold weight, and tight or absent letter-spacing.

Technical annotations (IBM Plex Mono)

Beyond eyebrows, IBM Plex Mono is the voice for small technical labeling: standards and data labels (FHIR, HL7, MCP, REST), technical captions under diagrams or code-adjacent visuals, and small technical UI accents such as ticker labels. Use weight 400 for running annotation text and 500 for emphasized labels, at caption sizes. It is a support face only: never body copy, headings, or buttons.

Implementation: load https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=IBM+Plex+Mono:wght@400;500&display=swap and reference it via the token --mono: "IBM Plex Mono", monospace;.

Dates and times

When a graphic carries a date or a time, use these formats so event cards, webinar promos, and speaker graphics stay consistent. To attribute a person, see the Name lockup pattern.

  • Dates: abbreviated month, no period: Jan 4, 2026. Ranges use a hyphen with no spaces: Jan 1-4, 2026.
  • Times: lowercase a.m./p.m. with periods, hyphenated range, time zone after: 10-11 a.m. EST.
  • Multiple time zones separate with a pipe: 10-11 a.m. EST | 9-10 a.m. CST.

Two-tone headline

In a two-tone headline, set only the word or two you are emphasizing in the accent color. Every other word, and the supporting description below, stays white or black depending on the background. On light backgrounds the accent is Rhapsody Blue (#1A81F4) against navy or black text. On dark backgrounds it is also Rhapsody Blue at headline size, where it stays vibrant on navy; drop to light blue (#B4D8FF) only when the accent is small. The description line never takes the accent color.

Use it sparingly

The two-tone headline exists to pull the eye to genuinely meaningful text. Highlight one idea per headline, and don't reach for it on every headline: if everything is highlighted, nothing is. When in doubt, set the whole headline in a single color and save the accent for the moment that matters.

Health data, finally connected
On dark: at headline size the emphasis word is Rhapsody Blue; the rest of the headline and this description stay white.
Health data, finally connected
On light: the emphasis word is Rhapsody Blue; the rest and this description stay navy or black.
Do
  • Color only the one or two words carrying the emphasis.
  • Keep the rest of the headline, and the description, white (on dark) or navy/black (on light).
  • Reserve it for headlines where the highlighted idea genuinely matters.
Don’t
  • Color the whole headline, or the description line, in the accent.
  • Highlight several words, so the emphasis is diluted.
  • Apply it to every headline across a layout or deck.

Leading & tracking

Line height (leading) and letter-spacing (tracking) keep the type feeling calm and open. Keep typography consistent by using the role-based settings below.

Text roleLine heightTrackingRule
Hero / H1110%Default (0)Keep large headlines compact and intentional.
H2 / H3120%Default (0)Use consistently across a layout.
Body150%Default (0)Prioritize comfortable reading.
Caption / support140–150%Default (0)Do not compress small text.
IBM Plex Mono eyebrow120%+0.16emThe deliberate exception for technical/all-caps labeling.
Do not manually tighten or loosen Poppins to make copy fit. Edit the copy, resize the type within the approved scale, or adjust the layout instead.

Minimum font size (web)

For legibility on screen, keep body and interface text at a readable minimum. These are floors, not targets, most body copy should sit comfortably above them.

  • Body copy: at least 16px on web. This is the baseline for comfortable reading.
  • Secondary and supporting text: at least 14px.
  • Captions, labels, and fine print: at least 12px. Do not go below 12px for anything a user needs to read.
  • Legal or disclaimer text: at least 11px, used only where unavoidable.
  • Maintain at least 3:1 contrast for large text and 4.5:1 for normal body text, so size and contrast work together.

Logo

The Rhapsody wordmark is the core of the identity. Lead with the primary version wherever possible; the alternates exist for dark backgrounds, one-color use, and tight spaces.

Variations

Four versions across light and dark backgrounds: the full-color wordmark and a one-color version of each.

On light
On dark
Primary: navy bar, blue wordmark. The bar is Rhapsody Navy (#0B2C47), not black.
Blue wordmark, white line. The two-color version for navy and dark backgrounds, at larger sizes only, about 240px / 2.25in wide and up, where the Rhapsody-blue wordmark stays vibrant. Below that size, use the all-white version instead.
One-color navy, for light or limited-color use.
All white. The default on navy and dark backgrounds at smaller sizes, and for one-color or limited-color use.

Monogram

The R monogram, for tight spaces only, social avatars, favicons, merch. Light version on light backgrounds; for dark mode the blue R keeps its color with a white bar (matching the wordmark’s blue letters and white accent). Never in place of the full logo in formal communications.

Logo rules

  • Clear spaceAlways keep clear space around the logo to protect its clarity. Use the height of the mark as the minimum clearance on all sides.
  • Minimum size, printNever smaller than 1.5 in / 38.1 mm wide.
  • Minimum size, web and videoNever smaller than 108 pixels wide.

In short

  • Navy bar and blue wordmark on light. On navy or dark backgrounds, use the blue-wordmark / white-line version at larger sizes; below the size threshold above, use the all-white wordmark.
  • Never the all-blue wordmark on navy at small sizes (low contrast); drop to all-white.
  • One-color navy or white for limited-color contexts.
  • Always all capital letters. Maintain clear space. Use official logo files only.

Product logo

Product logos pair the Rhapsody wordmark with a product name in a fixed lockup, horizontal or vertical. Use only approved lockups, never create product-only wordmarks or alter the mark.

Keep clear space of at least the height of the “R” on all sides. Mono, dark, and blue variants and all product names live in the product logo library (available on request from Rhapsody).

Co-branding lockup

For pairing the Rhapsody logo with a partner or customer logo, see Partner logos, which covers the co-branding lockup alongside the bracket treatment for logo walls and the rules for using another company’s logo.

Buttons and CTAs

Buttons are pill-shaped, set in Poppins Medium (500), sentence case, with a short action label like “Learn more” or “Request a demo.”

The pill shape

The pill is fully rounded: the corner radius equals half the button’s height, so the left and right ends are perfect semicircles. In CSS this is border-radius: 999px (any value at or above half the height produces the same full curve).

Do: full pill
Request a demo

Radius = ½ the height; the ends are perfect semicircles.

Don’t: partial radius
Request a demo

Partial corners read as a generic rounded rectangle, not the Rhapsody pill.

Primary and secondary

Primary is a filled pill and there is one per view: Rhapsody Blue with a white label on light and dark grounds alike (on navy the blue pill reads large and vibrant). The teal-filled pill is retired: it required a label set on teal, which the system no longer allows at any size. Secondary is the same pill as an outline, for a lower-priority action: white on dark, blue on light.

Primary · on dark
Request a demo
Primary · on light
Request a demo
Secondary · on dark
Learn more
Secondary · on light
Learn more
  • Fully rounded pill (see The pill shape); never a partial-radius rounded rectangle.
  • The pill radius is exclusive to CTAs: never use it to frame a module, card, chart, or image. For framing content, see Layout and spacing → Corners and shape.
  • Poppins Medium (500), sentence case, no bold (700).
  • Labels are short and action-led, and stay consistent through a flow.
  • Keep to no more than three brand colors in the surrounding layout.
  • Give buttons clear padding and space; do not place dots or graphics over them.

Text links and the CTA arrow

Text-style CTAs (“actionlinks”) end with a trailing right arrow (a leading space, then →), signaling forward movement into a deeper page. Pill buttons never take an arrow.

On light
Explore the platform →
On dark
Learn more →
Do: arrow on a text link
See how SimonMed did it →
Don’t: arrow on a button
Book a demo →
  • Text links only, “Explore …”, “Meet …”, “Learn more”, card CTAs, inline nav.
  • Use the arrow character &rarr; (→), one per link, always trailing with a leading space, never ->, », or an icon.
  • The arrow takes the link’s color, which follows its ground: on light, links are Rhapsody Blue (teal type never sits on light grounds — see Color → Teal in small applications); on navy, white, light blue, or teal per context; never orange.

Charts and graphs

Data visuals follow the same rules as everything else: brand colors, generous space, and no decoration. Lead with the point.

Charts and graphs

Grouped bar (two series): Rhapsody Blue paired with navy, light gridlines, navy title.

Line (three or more series): the order blue, teal, purple, orange, labeled directly.

Stacked bar: the order (blue, teal, purple, orange), only as many as the data needs; dark labels on the orange segment.

Donut: segments in order (blue, teal, purple, orange, light blue, navy); gray for the remainder; key number in the center.

Chart color order

Assign chart colors in the fixed order below so every chart reads as one system, adding only as many as the data needs. This data-series order matches the same color order as Pathways to promote design system consistency.

1 · Blue
2 · Teal
3 · Purple
4 · Orange
5 · Light blue
6 · Navy
Gray · remainder

Color rules in charts

  • Two series: Rhapsody Blue + navy, the cleanest, highest-contrast pairing. Use it whenever a chart compares just two things.
  • Three or more: follow the order blue, teal, purple, orange, light blue, navy, adding a color only when the data needs distinguishing.
  • Light blue is for fills and large areas (bar, stacked, and donut segments), not thin lines or small marks on white, where it is too low-contrast. On navy it reads at any size.
  • Orange is the fourth series color, and otherwise a sparing accent, never a whole palette of orange. Put dark (navy or black) labels on orange fills.
  • Purple is the third series color; don’t set purple as labels on navy or black.
  • Teal fills take dark labels only (navy or black), never white.
  • Gray (#D9DFE6) is the remainder or context series, and the gridline color. Titles navy, axis labels dark gray.
  • Stay within the order and add a color only when the data needs distinguishing; charts are the one place the three-color rule relaxes.

Chart style

  • No gradients, 3D, drop shadows, or heavy outlines. Data first.
  • Label directly where possible; legends are fine when they aid clarity.
  • Keep only the left (value) and bottom (category) axis lines. Drop the top and right sides of the plot frame so the chart isn’t boxed in—those lines carry no data and just add clutter.

Partner logos

When to use customer and partner logos

A customer or partner logo is fine to use once you’ve confirmed it meets the checklist below. How you place it depends on the situation:

  • Two or more logos: use the bracket treatment (the parenthesis device) so a mixed wall stays consistent in size and color.
  • A single customer logo: it can stand alone in the layout.
  • A partner logo: use the co-branding lockup (below) to place it alongside the Rhapsody logo, rather than on its own.

Bracket treatment for partner logos

To present a wall of customer or partner logos, place each logo between two curved brackets, echoing the connection motif without hard boxes. This keeps a busy multi-logo grid feeling refined and premium. The parenthesis device brings Rhapsody branding to multi-logo layouts and gives logos of different sizes and shapes (stacked versus horizontal) a consistent frame.

  • Two thin single-color arcs, one on each side of the logo, like parentheses.
  • Arc colors are blue, teal, and purple only. One color per logo.
  • Alternate the three colors across the set so no two neighbors match.
  • Place the partner logo in its own colors, centered and clear, between the arcs.
  • Fix one arc size for the whole wall. The bracket is a shared frame, so every pair of arcs is identical in height, curvature, gap, and stroke weight—only the color changes. Pick the arc height once (the frame), then fit every logo to it.
  • Size the logo to the arcs, not the reverse. Cap each logo’s optical height to about two-thirds of the arc height, centered between the arcs with equal clear space above and below, and hold a consistent gap of about 10% of the arc height between each arc and the logo so nothing touches.
  • Stroke weight: thin and uniform, about 1/18 of the arc height (roughly 5–6%), the same on every arc in the set.

Before using a partner or customer logo

Before placing a partner or customer logo, verify all of the following:

  • Correct, current version. Confirm it is the most recent, official version of the logo, not an outdated or unofficial mark.
  • Permission. Confirm we have permission to use the logo.
  • High resolution. The file is sharp at its display size, with no pixelation or artifacts.
  • Correct spacing. It sits within the brackets with clear space per guideline; never crowded or stretched.
  • Transparent background. Use a transparent-background file so the logo sits cleanly on the layout, never on its own white or colored box.

Co-branding lockup

When Rhapsody appears alongside a partner or customer logo, use a horizontal lockup: the Rhapsody wordmark, a thin teal divider, then the partner mark. The divider does the separating, so neither logo needs a box.

  • One thin teal divider, roughly the cap height of the wordmark. Never a box or rule around either logo.
  • Equal clear space on both sides; balance the two marks by eye, not pixel-for-pixel.
  • The lockup pairs Rhapsody with a single partner. To present a set of partner or customer logos together, use the bracket treatment above.

Quotes & testimonials

Proof points work hardest when they are short: cut quotes to a single powerful snippet and stats to the takeaway, then let the number or the line carry the weight.

Quotes

  • Reduce to one short, powerful line—cut everything that is not the point. Caps: one-line snippets under 60 characters, longer testimonials under 120; if a quote needs more, it needs editing.
  • Set it large using primary or secondary colors only, Rhapsody Blue or navy on light backgrounds, Rhapsody Blue on dark, never the tertiary purple or orange. Hold one accent color across a group of quotes or stats.
  • Highlight in a Rhapsody-colored box with white text, or Rhapsody-colored text on white.
  • Attribution: use the customer’s verified logo (accurate, current, high-res, transparent background) whenever we can; name the customer in small caps only when the logo can’t be used. For several logos, use the bracket treatment.
  • Always wrap the quote copy in opening and closing quotation marks. An oversized decorative mark is an optional accent, not a substitute for them.

For a longer, single-customer testimonial presented as a landscape banner (with the quote on navy and a light device), see the quote banner in Social posts.

Customer quote card

When a table needs color

Dot accents

Beyond the fluid dot pattern and the big dot (see Graphic devices), the dots can be composed into small decorative accents. These are a lighter, more graphic use of the motif—not a substitute for the primary devices.

Framing and diagram elements

The dots can be composed into shapes, a ring, an arc, or a network, that frame content or carry a simple idea. Use them as decorative and structural accents in creative work: digital display ads, white papers and reports, banners, and slides. Here the dots are always equal size, always multicolor but never orange, and carry no gradient fill. A faint connecting line is allowed for a diagram, never a squiggle.

Dot row accent

A short horizontal row of dots is an approved compact use of the dot motif, useful in banners and email headers where the full fluid pattern would be too much.

  • A few dots, one uniform size, evenly spaced.
  • Sequence through brand colors, for example teal, blue, light blue, purple.
  • Use as a small accent, not a full field. Do not combine with the fluid dot pattern in the same layout.

Graphic devices at a glance

Rhapsody works from one connected family of visual devices. Each carries a distinct meaning and a recommended color lead, so the device reinforces the message rather than just decorating it.

The device system is intentionally limited. Fewer choices create a more recognizable, premium brand and make AI-generated work more consistent. Usually lead with one visual expression per layout, but the evolved devices can be combined with restraint when it genuinely helps (see below).

Device Meaning Why / when to use
Aurora When everything comes together, harmony across the system. Allows movement. The one light device, with range from a soft wash to a flowing form. Use for harmony, ease, and connected systems, and for motion, video, animated headers, and large backdrops. Navy or dark backgrounds only.
Fluid dot pattern Scale and order, data resolving into one connected field. Use to communicate data, infrastructure, scale, and systems working together. A half-tone dot grid that flows dense-to-sparse; best for larger compositions where the graphic can occupy its own visual space.
Big dot Relationship and momentum, systems of every size connecting. Use for simple, high-impact brand moments where a full graphic field would be too complex. Best for small or fast-read formats, hero moments, and compositions that need a strong visual anchor.
Photography The human industry we serve, people first. Use when people, expertise, collaboration, or real-world technology environments strengthen the story. Photography should make Rhapsody feel credible, modern, and human while balancing the more abstract graphic devices.
Master-art rule

Do not recreate or alter graphic devices. Use the approved SVG/PNG master art as provided.

Combine with restraint

Lead with one device by default, but the evolved devices can work together when it makes sense: a big dot alongside a photo, or the fluid dot pattern as a quiet background behind a photo, both pair well. Don’t overdo it, two complementary elements at most, never a stack of devices competing for attention, and nothing placed over faces or copy. If a layout feels empty, prefer open space over adding decoration.

Fluid dot pattern

One of the two dot devices; see Big dot for when to use the pattern versus the big dot, and for the background → dot-color rules. The fluid dot pattern is a half-tone dot grid: identical dots on one grid that gather into a dense core at an edge or corner and dissolve fluidly outward, each dot easing from large to small so the field flows rather than stops. It carries the same meaning as before, many separate points resolving into one connected, legible field, in a more refined, fluid register. It never forms a recognizable object, symbol, letter, line, or shape.

A closed, approved family, use it, don’t build it

The patterns are a closed, approved set, one for each background, anchor, and format, shipped as transparent SVG, 2× PNG, and on-ground JPG. Pick the file that fits and use it as-is, flipped, or rotated 90°. Do not hand-place a new pattern or restyle one, no recoloring, resizing individual dots, gradients, opacity, strokes, or non-proportional stretching.

Registers

Each master is built for one background, which sets the dot colors (see Dots overview). Keep copy in the clear area opposite the dense core, and use one pattern per layout.

White on navy. The default dark register; core at a corner or edge.

White on Rhapsody blue. White dots only on a blue ground.

Dots on white. Navy or Rhapsody-blue dots on a light ground.

Multicolor on navy. Blue, light blue, teal, purple, white, plus up to three orange.

The rules for the fluid dot pattern

Clearance is the rule most often broken. No copy, headline, button, card, logo, or image sits on top of the pattern, and nothing crops one. Keep copy in the clear area opposite the dense core, cover no more than 50 percent of the space, and use one dot device per layout, never two patterns, and never a pattern with the big dot or a light device.

At a glance: do and don’t

On-brand
  • An approved fluid pattern on white, Rhapsody blue, or navy, used as-is, flipped, or rotated 90°.
  • Single color or multicolor; multicolor includes up to three orange dots.
  • Dense core anchored to a corner or edge, with a clear gap from text.
  • The one dot device in the layout, anchored and used verbatim.
Off-brand
  • Full-view takeover or more than 50 percent coverage.
  • Hand-built grids, mixed dot sizes, or dots over text, faces, or the logo.
  • Off-palette, outlined, or gradient-filled dots; recolored masters.
  • Two patterns at once, or a pattern paired with the big dot or a light device.

Masters (transparent SVG + 2× PNG + on-ground JPG), used verbatim or flipped/rotated: Fluid Dot Pattern. The earlier scattered/structured dot field is retired (see Quick corrections log).

Big dot

The dots are Rhapsody’s primary graphic device, and they carry the meaning of what we do: each dot is a data point, a system, a person, and Rhapsody connects, cleans, and orders them. Two compositions tell that story, the fluid dot pattern (its own card) for large canvases, and the big dot for compact, high-impact moments. The big dot is one dominant circle cropped by two edges, the anchor, with two to four smaller companions gathering and overlapping around it. The varied sizes are organizations of every scale; the overlap is the point, separate systems touching and exchanging, with Rhapsody as the anchoring dot the others connect around.

A closed, approved family, use it, don’t build it

The big dots are a closed, approved ecosystem, one set per background with three crops each, shipped as transparent SVG and 1×/2× PNG and JPG. Use one as-is, flipped, or rotated 90°; never hand-build, recolor, or restyle it.

Fluid pattern or big dot?

Use one dot device per layout, never both, and never a dot device with a light device. Reach for the fluid dot pattern on larger canvases with room to breathe, full or section backgrounds, web heroes, slide and report covers, where the pattern can dissolve gradually from an edge. Reach for the big dot on small, fast-read formats, display ads, social tiles, thin banners, cover slides, plus hero and brand moments that want warmth. The decorative dot accents are a separate, lighter use.

The ecosystem

One anchor cropped by two edges plus two to four companions, built for each ground in three crops (top, bottom, and side). Pick the file that fits the layout and crop.

On navy
On Rhapsody blue
On white
What the parts mean

The parts map to the two-pillar story: the anchor is Rhapsody; larger companions are the systems it connects (Build the infrastructure); smaller companions are the agents across them (Automate the work). An optional single orange outlier can mark the next system, not yet connected, use it at most once and omit it when the message claims completeness (“every,” “all,” a finished total).

Backgrounds and dot colors

Each set is built for one background and is not interchangeable. The anchor is never the background hue; purple and orange stay on the companions, never the anchor.

GroundAnchorCompanions
NavyRhapsody blueWhite, light blue, teal
Rhapsody blueNavy, white, or light blueWhite, navy, light blue, teal, purple
WhiteNavy or Rhapsody blueRhapsody blue, light blue, teal, navy, purple

The fluid dot pattern keeps its own registers (white on navy, white on blue, dots on white, multicolor on navy), detailed on its card. Orange lives in the fluid multicolor field only, never on a blue ground, and never more than 3 dots so it reads as a surprise. The dots are exempt from the three-color rule.

  • Anchor, cropped by two edges (about 25–45% off-frame) so it’s never a whole circle floating in the frame.
  • Companions, 2–4, all different sizes. They may overlap the anchor but never each other; each stays a distinct, readable circle.
  • Flat fill, perfect circles, no gradient, opacity, or stroke.
  • Copy on the calm side, clear of the dots by at least one large-companion diameter; nothing sits on or crops the dots.
  • One device per layout, big dot or fluid pattern, never both, and never with a light device. Cover no more than 50% of the space. Formats: 16×9 (cover slides, web hero, video), 1×1 (social tile), 9×16 (story, vertical video), and a 728×90 thin banner.

Masters (transparent SVG + 1×/2× PNG + JPG), used verbatim or flipped/rotated: included in this package (rhapsody-brand-assets/dot-devices).

Light devices

Alongside the dots, Aurora is the light device, and the only one. Where the dots are precise and rational, Aurora is warm and human, together they say engineered, but human. It is a single device with range: from a calm, soft wash to a flowing band of light. Aurora allows movement, so the same device covers both still and moving work. Use it for photo-free digital moments like heroes, social, slides, and video.

Rules for Aurora

Aurora sits on navy grounds only. On any other background, Rhapsody Blue, white, or a photograph, don’t use a glow, use the dots device or photography instead. The glow uses teal, blue, and purple only, never orange, and stays within three colors. Offset the glow into open space so copy sits on the calm side of the composition, never on the brightest point.

One device, soft to flowing

Soft wash. A calm, blended glow. When everything comes together, harmony across the system. The everyday register.

Flowing. A band of light with movement, for motion, video, animated headers, and large hero or event backdrops. The same Aurora, with more energy.

Glow color

Aurora is teal-led (see Devices at a glance), and can run through teal, blue, and purple. Within that, the exact blend is left to design, always within the teal / blue / purple glow palette, following the color hierarchy and staying legible on the navy ground.

Movement

Aurora is allowed to move. For motion and large-scale applications, video, animated headers, and large hero or event backdrops, lean into the flowing form, where it has room to move and is not hugging copy. It is a great way to suggest our AI capabilities, modern, fluid, and seamless, without being literal. For everyday layouts, banners, and anywhere text sits close, keep to the calmer wash.

Master files for Aurora (soft and flowing; transparent PNG and on-navy JPG): AuroraGlow.

Aurora in use

Aurora leads a layout with the copy on the calm side, clear of the glow. The banner below shows Aurora on navy; the same glow leads the Social posts quote banner and the Product launch announcement.

  • Teal, blue, purple only; never orange.
  • Navy grounds only. Digital hero, social, slide, and video atmosphere. Not behind photography, and not a universal print element.
  • Maintain a clear margin of about 6 to 7 percent of the shorter side around the composition.
  • Use one graphic device, dots or Aurora, per layout, not both at once.

Icon library

Rhapsody uses a single, consistent family of outline (line) icons: simple geometric shapes drawn as strokes, not filled shapes. The reference implementation is the feature-card icon set on the “How we compare” page (building, code brackets, grid, eye, lock, bell). Think Lucide / Feather style: clean, minimal, single-weight.

The reference set

Icon drawing spec

  • Canvas: 24×24 viewBox.
  • Style: fill="none", stroke only. Never use filled/solid glyphs or duotone.
  • Stroke: stroke-width="1.7", rounded line caps and joins (stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round").
  • Color: set stroke to currentColor so the icon inherits the surrounding text/context color and adapts automatically (blue on light, white or light on dark). Do not hardcode hex on decorative icons.
  • One concept per icon; keep detail minimal so it stays legible at small sizes.

The icon tile

Feature and benefit icons always sit in the approved 44×44 rounded-square tile with an 11px corner radius. The icon renders at 22×22, centered. Use exactly one of the two treatments below; do not invent alternate tile colors or use uncontained icons for features/benefits.

Light-background tile

Tile #E9EEF4 · icon Rhapsody Blue #1A81F4.

Dark-background tile

Tile white at 10% opacity · icon Light Blue #B4D8FF.

  • Use the light treatment on white, light gray, and gray-blue surfaces.
  • Use the dark treatment on Rhapsody Navy and other approved dark surfaces.
  • Icons remain in the blue family only; never teal, purple, or orange.
  • Functional marks such as checks/crosses remain the exception below.

Functional marks

Yes/no indicators in comparison tables are the exception to the tile treatment: a check in Rhapsody blue (#1A81F4) and a cross in muted gray (#7E858C), both at stroke-width 3 for weight. These are UI marks, not decorative icons, and don’t sit in tiles.

Included Not included

Don’ts

  • No mixing icon families.
  • No varying stroke weights within an icon set.
  • No drop shadows or gradients on icons.
  • No emoji as icons.

Legacy two-color icons in the Rhapsody icon library (available on request from Rhapsody) are for existing assets only; new work uses the outline family above.

Illustrations

The previous character-driven illustration style is retired for new work. It does not support the more mature, technology-forward position Rhapsody needs with enterprise buyers, partners, and investors.

Prefer
  • Real photography and credible technical environments.
  • Product/interface imagery and software shown in context.
  • Data visualization, architecture diagrams, and system maps.
  • Approved graphic devices.
Avoid
  • Cartoon people, whimsical scenes, cute metaphors, or character-driven spot illustrations.
  • Generic robot heads, glowing brains, humanoid AI figures, circuit-board faces, or hologram clichés.
  • Decorative sparkles or “AI magic” motifs used without a specific brand-system reason.

Photography

Imagery reflects a modern SaaS company serving a high-stakes, regulated, human industry. Show the systems, teams, technology, and software environments that make care possible, not hospital care itself. The overall impression is confident, open, collaborative, technically credible, and current.

Technology credibility

Balance human imagery with credible technical context: integration teams, developers, enterprise environments, product interfaces, system monitoring, collaborative technical work, and data infrastructure. Avoid relying on generic smiling-office photography as the only human expression of the brand.

People come first

Photography is a co-equal brand expression, not decoration. Real people, teams, and faces should carry our work as much as any graphic device. When a layout could hold either a person or an abstract device, lead with the person: the dots and glows are the accent to a human story, not a replacement for it. Proportion cue: across a page, campaign, or deck, people should lead at least as often as a device.

Approved library examples: forward-facing, genuine, modern workspaces, inclusive across roles and ages.

Use

  • People facing the camera or each other, eye contact, active discussion.
  • Faces sharp and eyes visible; soft, even lighting.
  • Inclusive representation across roles, ages, and identities.
  • Modern workspaces with visible data or code; bright, natural light.
  • Clean backgrounds and consistent color temperature across a page.

Avoid

  • Dark, dim, or tech-noir treatments.
  • Motion blur or soft-focus faces.
  • Harsh light flaring toward the camera.
  • Backs to camera, staged handshakes, stiff poses.
  • Literal hospital-care scenes; overly retouched or generic stock.

Portrait treatments

For real people, employees, webinar speakers, and customers, use one of these treatments, the approved standard for portraits.

  • Default to the brand ring: a bold navy ring with a thin Rhapsody-Blue outer edge, the website-hero weight, around a circular crop (the same family as Hero badge graphics). For an accent variant, swap the outer edge to one brand color per portrait, primary or secondary only, chosen for contrast against the background, Rhapsody Blue or navy on light grounds, light blue or teal on dark. Never the tertiary purple or orange. Hold the one color consistent across a set.
  • Bright, forward-facing photo, cropped to face and shoulders, on a clean light background, with generous white space.
  • Keep the ring clean and even all the way around. Avoid white rings, drop shadows, or busy backgrounds behind the portrait.

Hero badge graphics

The hero badge is Rhapsody’s signature treatment for website heroes, product pages, and market-segment pages: a circular image (a person photo, or a product / segment illustration) held by a thick Rhapsody-Blue ring, sitting on the fluid dot pattern, with small rounded-square icon badges tagging what the system does. It is the same dot device used everywhere else, here it simply sits behind the image.

Built from the fluid dot pattern

The dots around the badge are the fluid dot pattern (see Fluid dot pattern), placed behind the image and fading out so it never ends in a hard edge. The badge is a focal device, one per hero, that lets a photo or illustration sit inside the brand system instead of floating on its own. It is not a separate “halo” device.

The treatment

Established on the website heroes. Treat it as the reference for ring weight, the image crop, and how the fluid dot pattern sits behind.

Anatomy

  • Image. A circular crop, centered: a person photo, or a single white-and-light-blue product / segment illustration on navy.
  • Ring. Navy fill (#0B2C47) with a Rhapsody-Blue stroke (#1A81F4): a bold navy band with an ~8px blue outer edge, even all the way around.
  • Fluid dot pattern behind. The approved fluid dot pattern sits behind the image (light blue / blue dots), fading out so it never ends in a square or cropped edge. Never a radial “halo” built by hand.
  • Icon badges (optional). Small rounded squares on the ring that tag a capability. Two per badge at most, at opposite corners, clear of the face.

Two fills

One badge system, two jobs. Photos carry people, customers, teams, homepage and CTA heroes. Illustrations carry products and market segments, a single white-and-light-blue illustration on the navy disc (drawn from the hero illustration library).

Icon badges

Optional capability tags on the ring. Use at most two, in the two weights below, to signal a feature (security, exchange, automation). They are rounded squares (the signature corner), never circles; keep them off faces and clear of the densest dots.

Light badge
White fill, blue ring, blue icon
Dark badge
Blue fill, white ring, white icon
Do
  • Put the fluid dot pattern behind the image and let it fade softly to nothing.
  • One badge per hero; photo for people, illustration for products and segments.
  • Keep the ring even; center the image in the disc.
  • Hold icon badges to two rounded squares, at opposite corners, clear of the face.
Don’t
  • Don’t hand-build a radial dot “halo,” or crop the pattern to a hard edge.
  • Don’t recolor the ring; it stays navy with the blue edge.
  • Don’t make the icon badges circles, or stack more than two.
  • Don’t mix a photo and an illustration inside one badge.
Master-art rule

Use the approved hero-badge master art (photo rings and segment illustrations) and the fluid dot pattern masters as provided. Recreate the ring and the dot backdrop only from the spec above when a live element is genuinely needed.

Display ads

Display units are billboard-simple: Rhapsody Blue leads (it reads best in display; navy is the occasional alternate), the logo is prominent, a few large words carry one quick read, and there is one action. The full system is available, but restraint wins the placement. One in-context example is shown below; exhaustive per-size placement specs live with the paid-media team, not in this guideline.

In context

  • Blue-first ground. Rhapsody Blue is the default; navy is the occasional alternate. White logo on both.
  • Logo leads, always. The wordmark is prominent in every unit; use the monogram only where the wordmark won’t fit (≤50px tall). Never small or buried.
  • Few, large words. Billboard logic, a short headline read in seconds. Cut words before you shrink type; 13px floor at delivered size.
  • One device, one action. One device max, photo, fluid dot pattern, big dot, or nothing, clear of the copy, and a single CTA (a pill, or an arrow chip in tight formats).
Keep it to one read

If a unit needs more than a glance, it’s doing too much. Trim to the logo, one line, and one action; let the blue ground and a single device do the rest.

Templates

PowerPoint deck template

The official Rhapsody slide deck template (2026), on the current brand: Poppins for headings and body, IBM Plex Mono eyebrows, Rhapsody Navy #0B2C47 grounds, and the approved layout catalog (title, agenda, content, data, quote, timeline, stats and closing slides). It is a PowerPoint file you download and edit in PowerPoint, not a web component — build decks from it rather than from a blank file.

Download

Master file: downloads/Rhapsody-PowerPoint-Template-2026.pptx — 65 slides. Start every Rhapsody deck from this template; never rebuild the layouts, colors or type.

Using it

  • Pick a layout from the catalog and fill in content — don’t alter colors, fonts, or structural elements.
  • Poppins Light/Regular for body, Medium for emphasis; eyebrows and labels in IBM Plex Mono.
  • Keep to three brand colors per slide; flat color only, no gradients.
  • White logo on navy/blue grounds, blue-black logo on light.

The web design system (these cards) governs color, type, logo, devices and patterns; this deck applies that system to slides. For digital display formats see Display ads.

Email signature

A consistent employee signature keeps everyday email on brand. Keep it text-based and simple so it renders in every client: the wordmark, a thin teal divider, then the name lockup and contact lines. Use Poppins where the client supports it, with Arial as the fallback. Set copy in navy, dark gray, and Rhapsody Blue on a white background; don’t add background colors, images behind text, or quotes.

Building for email

  • Subject & preheader. One clear subject in brand voice, front-loading the value (around 40 characters); write the preheader as a real complement to it, never “View in browser.”
  • Images off by default. Many clients block images, so never lock the core message or the CTA inside an image. Set the headline and button as live HTML text, and give every image alt text, including the wordmark.
  • Width. Keep the content column around 600px so it renders reliably across clients and on mobile.
  • Dark mode. Assume some clients recolor. The navy header with the white wordmark (transparent PNG) holds up; avoid dark type on transparent PNGs that can invert into dark-on-dark.

Pardot & client rendering

  • Build for Pardot (Account Engagement). Use a table-based layout with inline styles (like the signature), a single ~600px column, and hosted images in Pardot. Include the required merge fields, unsubscribe link and mailing address, and keep handlebars/merge tokens out of the visible design.
  • Fonts degrade, don’t embed. Poppins won’t load in most inboxes, so set font-family:'Poppins',Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif and design so the Arial fallback still looks right. Don’t ship copy baked into images to force the font.
  • Outlook (Windows) uses Word to render. Stick to tables, avoid CSS background-image (put the navy header color on a table cell, with the glow/dots as a hosted image), and expect border-radius to square off, so use bulletproof table-cell buttons (VML for a rounded pill) rather than a CSS pill.
  • Gmail. Keep the HTML lean, Gmail clips messages over ~102KB (“View entire message”) and favors inline styles. Test in Gmail web and the mobile app alongside Outlook.

Quick corrections log

✕ RETIRED

Do not use

Treatments from the earlier brand guide, retired for all new work. No exceptions.

  • Busy circle / photo / icon-overlay montages — the composite hero of headshots orbiting an illustration with floating speech bubbles and shapes. Use real photography with the modern treatments, the fluid dot pattern, or an approved Aurora master.
  • Legacy line-art / spot illustrations and character-driven cartoon scenes — including outlined “person + cloud + lock” artwork, whimsical people, and juvenile spot illustrations. Replace with photography, product/interface imagery, diagrams, data visualization, or approved abstract devices.
  • Two-tone / two-color icons — including icon-on-circle art. Replaced by the single outline family (stroke-only, 1.7 weight, currentColor).
  • Thick color rings around headshots / people — no thick ring anywhere, no exceptions. Portraits use the thin ring, arc accent, rounded-rectangle card, or editorial split.
  • Squiggle line with dots — the wandering hairline path with colored nodes. Use the fluid dot pattern or Aurora.
  • Burst and Plexus light devices — retired. The light device is now Aurora only (one glow, soft to flowing). Anywhere Burst or Plexus appeared, use the Aurora glow.
  • Scattered / structured dot field (the earlier 45-composition grid family) — retired and replaced by the Fluid dot pattern. Use the approved fluid-pattern masters; don’t reuse the old df-* field art.
  • Aurora ribbon as a separate register — retired as a distinct item. Aurora is now one device that allows movement; the flowing form is part of it, not a second device.

Changelog (October 2026)

  • Scattered dot field replaced by the Fluid dot pattern. The structured scattered field is retired across the system. Its successor is the Fluid dot pattern, a half-tone dot grid that flows dense-to-sparse, with the same registers (white on navy, white on blue, dots on white, multicolor on navy). New verbatim masters live in Devices → Fluid Dot Pattern; the old df-* field art is removed.
  • Aurora merged into one device. The Aurora wash and the Aurora ribbon are no longer two registers; Aurora is a single light device that allows movement, from a soft wash to a flowing form. New verbatim Aurora masters folded in. Still navy-only, teal-led, teal / blue / purple.
  • Light devices reduced to Aurora. Burst and Plexus are retired. Everywhere Burst or Plexus was used (product launch, social quote banner, devices overview), switch to the Aurora glow.

Latest updates (October 2026)

  • Teal is immutable. Small teal applications on light grounds were failing contrast checks and getting darkened in production — creating off-brand second teals. The ruling: #23C5BF is the only teal, never darkened, tinted, or theme-converted to pass a check. When a teal application fails contrast, change the ground or the role, never the hex. Full rules and demos in Color → Teal in small applications.
  • Teal type on navy only. Eyebrows, labels, actionlinks, and small icons may be teal on navy (6.7:1, passes at any size). On white or gray-blue there is no teal type: automation actionlinks stay Rhapsody Blue, and the teal cue is carried by an accent — the module accent line, the teal seam, or the new teal tick (a 16×3px teal bar before a navy mono label, the approved pattern for pathway-coded labels on light grounds). This scopes the July 2026 “teal actionlink in automation contexts” allowance below to dark grounds.
  • Teal-filled pill retired. The primary-on-dark button is a Rhapsody Blue fill with a white label; the teal pill required a label set on teal, which September 2026 removed at any size. See Buttons & CTAs.
  • Framework visuals on the web are built, not pictured. Concept and architecture diagrams on web pages are embedded as native, responsive HTML — real text that reflows at every width — never as an image inside a screenshot or browser frame. The framed-media treatment is reserved for what genuinely is a screen or artifact: product UI, demo video, an audit record, a sample deliverable. First application: the Build + Automate architecture framework on the Solutions pages (web-style.md §6, §9); the Claude Design image master remains the source for decks, PDFs, and social.

Direction confirmed, superseding earlier drafts

  • Multicolor dots are approved. Both white-on-blue and multicolor are equal, on-brand registers for digital and physical. An earlier draft wrongly labeled multicolor off-brand.
